rows: Solubility
Lower aliphatic amines: Soluble in water due to hydrogen bonding.
Solubility decreases with increasing molar mass due to the larger hydrophobic alkyl group.
Higher amines: Essentially insoluble in water.
Boiling Point
Primary and secondary amines: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding present.
Primary amines: Stronger association due to two hydrogen atoms for bonding.
Tertiary amines: No hydrogen bonding due to the absence of hydrogen atoms on nitrogen.
Order of Boiling Point
Primary > Secondary > Tertiary

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Classify the following amine as Primary, Secondary or Tertiary-
blocks.answer:
Tertiary (3°) Amine.

In the given compound, the nitrogen atom is directly bonded to:

  • Two methyl groups (-CH3)
  • An aromatic ring
Therefore, the nitrogen atom is directly bonded to three carbon groups.

Hence, the given amine is classified as a Tertiary (3°) Amine.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Melting points are normally the highest for

(1) Tertiary amides

(2) Secondary amides

(3) Primary amides

(4) Amines
blocks.answer:
Ans.  (3) Primary amides

Answer: (3) Primary amides

Melting points are generally the highest for primary amides because of the extensive hydrogen bonding between the amide molecules. The primary amides

(\( -CONH_2−​\)) have both \( -NH_2−​\)and carbonyl groups, allowing them to form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which require more energy to break.

Therefore, primary amides have maximum melting points.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text:
• Confusing primary, secondary, and tertiary amines.
  • Misunderstanding the basicity of amines and their comparison with ammonia.
  • Forgetting to consider the effect of substituents on amine basicity.
  • Incorrectly assigning IUPAC names or structural representations.
